title: Jira and Linear are legacy: build the prototype first, then write the spec
summary: Theo argues issue trackers were built for a human handoff model that AI agents are dissolving. He pushes his "prototype first, spec second" method from Twitch, says role-splitting and long planning no longer make sense with capable models, and sees automations as most valuable to non-developers.

principles.text: Build a quick prototype before writing the spec; the spec written afterward is far more accurate.
principles.quote: Make a first version of the thing, then make the spec, then build it correctly, rather than write a spec assuming you know how it will work, and build it wrong because you were incorrect with the spec

principles.text: A prototype's job is learning scope and testing worth, not shipping faster, but it often ships anyway.
principles.quote: the point of this process wasn't to get the feature out faster. It was to develop a working prototype of it to know what was required to do it and to make a better spec

principles.text: The first version is always flawed; build it to learn, throw it away, then build the good one now that code is cheap.
principles.quote: The first version of software will always be less than ideal. Do it first to figure it out, throw it away, and then make a good version after.

principles.text: Role divisions existed because humans could do only one job; with capable AI they stop making sense.
principles.quote: My hot take is that the way we have broken up all these pieces made sense when humans did it and a given human could only do one of these things.

principles.text: Skip long multi-step planning; let the model build a first pass and use that as the plan.
principles.quote: There's no reason for planning to take hours. There's no reason for planning to fill your entire context.

principles.text: Non-developers adopt automation most readily because developers have trained themselves to skip it.
principles.quote: So, we've kind of trained our brains to ignore the urge to automate things that aren't super useful.
